blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Unit 4 (Matrices & Determinants), arranged by the unit's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation that shows the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The word matrix was first used by the English mathematician:
blocks.explanation: The word matrix was first used by James Sylvester (1814 - 1897); Arthur Cayley developed the theory of matrices.

book_ref.quote: the word matrix was first used by the English mathematician James Sylvester

blocks.prompt: 2 Who developed the theory of matrices and used them in linear transformations?
blocks.explanation: Arthur Cayley (1821 - 1895) developed the theory of matrices and used them in linear transformations.

book_ref.quote: developed the theory of matrices and used them in linear transformations

blocks.prompt: 3 The order of the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\) is:
blocks.explanation: It has 2 rows (horizontal lines) and 3 columns (vertical lines). Order is written rows first: \(2 \times 3\).

book_ref.quote: The horizontal lines of numbers are called rows and the vertical lines of numbers are called columns

blocks.prompt: 4 In the matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\), the entry \(a_{23}\) is:

blocks.explanation: An \(m \times n\) matrix has \(m \cdot n\) entries: \(4 \times 5 = 20\).

blocks.prompt: 6 A matrix in which the number of rows is not equal to the number of columns is called a:
blocks.explanation: If \(m \ne n\), the matrix of order \(m \times n\) is a rectangular matrix.

book_ref.quote: a matrix in which the number of rows is not equal to the number of columns is said to be a rectangular matrix

blocks.prompt: 7 The matrix \(\begin{bmatrix}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}\) is a:
blocks.explanation: All entries off the principal diagonal are 0 and all diagonal entries equal the same non-zero number \(k = 5\): a scalar matrix. It is not the unit matrix because \(5 \ne 1\).

book_ref.quote: is called a scalar matrix of order

blocks.prompt: 8 Which of the following is a diagonal matrix?
blocks.explanation: A diagonal matrix has \(a_{ij} = 0\) for \(i \ne j\) and at least one diagonal entry non-zero. \(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}\) qualifies; the null matrix fails because all its diagonal entries are 0.

book_ref.quote: may be zero but not all, then the matrix

blocks.prompt: 9 The entries of the secondary diagonal of \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8 & 9\end{bmatrix}\) are:
blocks.explanation: The secondary diagonal is \(a_{13}, a_{22}, a_{31}\) (top-right to bottom-left): \(3, 5, 7\). \(1, 5, 9\) is the principal diagonal.

book_ref.quote: form the secondary diagonal of

blocks.prompt: 10 A scalar matrix whose diagonal entries are all equal to \(k\) is the unit (identity) matrix when \(k\) equals:
blocks.explanation: The unit matrix has \(a_{ij} = 0\) for \(i \ne j\) and \(a_{ij} = 1\) for \(i = j\): a scalar matrix with \(k = 1\).

book_ref.quote: is called a unit matrix or identity matrix of order

blocks.prompt: 11 If \(\begin{bmatrix}x + 1 & 3 \\ 2 & y - 2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}\), then:
blocks.explanation: Equal matrices have equal corresponding entries: \(x + 1 = 4 \Rightarrow x = 3\) and \(y - 2 = 5 \Rightarrow y = 7\).

book_ref.quote: Two matrices of the same order are said to be equal if their corresponding entries are equal

blocks.prompt: 12 If \(A\) is a matrix of order \(2 \times 5\), then the order of \(A^{t}\) is:
blocks.explanation: The transpose interchanges rows and columns, so an \(m \times n\) matrix becomes \(n \times m\): \(5 \times 2\).

book_ref.quote: matrix obtained by interchanging the rows and columns of

blocks.prompt: 13 A matrix whose every element is zero is called a:
blocks.explanation: A square or rectangular matrix whose every element is zero is a null (zero) matrix; it may be of any order.

book_ref.quote: A square or rectangular matrix whose every element is zero is called a null or zero matrix

blocks.prompt: 14 Two matrices are conformable for addition if they:

options.text: have the same number of rows only
have the same number of entries

blocks.explanation: Addition is defined only for matrices of the same order. A \(2 \times 3\) and a \(3 \times 2\) matrix both have 6 entries but cannot be added.

book_ref.quote: Two matrices are conformable for addition if they are of the same order.

blocks.explanation: \(A - B = [a_{ij} - b_{ij}]\) and \(B - A = [b_{ij} - a_{ij}] = -(A - B)\). Subtraction is not commutative.

book_ref.quote: then we define the subtraction of

book_ref.quote: Obviously, the order of \(kA\) is \(m \times n\).

options.text: number of rows of \(A\) = number of rows of \(B\)
number of rows of \(A\) = number of columns of \(B\)
number of columns of \(A\) = number of rows of \(B\)

blocks.explanation: \((m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p\): \((3 \times 2)(2 \times 4) = 3 \times 4\).

blocks.text: 4.3 Properties of Matrix Addition, Scalar Multiplication and Matrix Multiplication

blocks.prompt: 27 The property \(A + B = B + A\) is called the:
blocks.explanation: \(A + B = B + A\) is the commutative property of matrix addition; it holds because each entry is an ordinary sum of numbers.

book_ref.quote: Commutative property w.r.t. addition

blocks.prompt: 28 For conformable matrices, \(A(BC) = (AB)C\) is the:
blocks.explanation: \(A(BC) = (AB)C\) is the associative property of matrix multiplication (property vii).

book_ref.quote: Associative property w.r.t. multiplication

blocks.prompt: 29 \(A(B + C) = AB + AC\) is called the:
blocks.explanation: \(A\) stays on the left: \(A(B + C) = AB + AC\) is the left distributive property; \((A + B)C = AC + BC\) is the right one.

book_ref.quote: Left distributive property

blocks.prompt: 30 Which of the following is NOT true in general for square matrices of the same order?
blocks.explanation: Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general. For example \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}7 & 9 \\ -2 & -4\end{bmatrix}\) but in the other order the product is \(\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\).

book_ref.quote: Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general.

blocks.prompt: 31 For scalars \(c, d\), the property \((c + d)A = cA + dA\) is the:
blocks.explanation: Property (vi)(b): \((c + d)A = cA + dA\) is a distributive property w.r.t. scalar multiplication; \((cd)A = c(dA)\) is the associative one.

book_ref.quote: Distributive property w.r.t. scalar multiplication

blocks.prompt: 32 In \(IA = AI = A\), the matrix \(I\) is the:
blocks.explanation: The unit matrix \(I\) is the multiplicative identity; the null matrix \(O\) is the additive identity (\(A + O = A\)).

book_ref.quote: Existence of multiplicative identity

blocks.prompt: 33 The value of \(\begin{vmatrix}4 & -3 \\ 2 & 5\end{vmatrix}\) is:

book_ref.quote: Multiply along the leading diagonal, then subtract the product along the other diagonal

blocks.prompt: 34 A determinant is defined for:
blocks.explanation: Only a square matrix has a determinant; a \(2 \times 3\) matrix has none.

book_ref.quote: Only a square matrix (same number of rows and columns) has a determinant

blocks.prompt: 35 If \(\begin{vmatrix}x & 2 \\ 3 & x\end{vmatrix} = 10\), then \(x\) equals:
blocks.explanation: \(x^{2} - 6 = 10 \Rightarrow x^{2} = 16 \Rightarrow x = \pm 4\).

book_ref.quote: Every determinant of order 3 will be reduced to determinants of order 2

blocks.text: 4.4.1 Minor and Cofactor of an Element of a Matrix or its Determinant

blocks.prompt: 36 The minor \(M_{ij}\) of an element \(a_{ij}\) is the determinant formed by deleting:
blocks.explanation: \(M_{ij}\) is the determinant left after deleting the row and the column through \(a_{ij}\): row \(i\) and column \(j\).

book_ref.quote: is the determinant formed by deleting the

book_ref.quote: For order 3 the signs form a chessboard pattern

blocks.prompt: 38 For the same \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\), the minor \(M_{23}\) is:
blocks.explanation: Delete row 2 and column 3: \(M_{23} = \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} = 8 - 1 = 7\). (The cofactor \(A_{23}\) is \(-7\); a minor has no extra sign.)

book_ref.quote: To find the minor of the element

blocks.prompt: 39 If \(i + j\) is odd, then the cofactor \(A_{ij}\) equals:

book_ref.quote: The cofactor of an element

blocks.prompt: 40 How many minors does a square matrix of order 3 have?
blocks.explanation: There is one minor for each element, and a matrix of order 3 has \(3 \times 3 = 9\) elements.

book_ref.quote: so a matrix of order 3 has 9 minors, one for each element

blocks.text: 4.4.2 Determinant of a Square Matrix of Order n = 3

blocks.prompt: 41 The value of \(\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 4 & 1\end{vmatrix}\) is:

book_ref.quote: Equation (vii) is the required expansion of determinant of square matrix of order 3.

blocks.prompt: 42 To save work, a determinant of order 3 is best expanded along the row or column that has:
blocks.explanation: Every row and column gives the same value; a zero element makes its whole term vanish, so choose the line with the most zeros.

book_ref.quote: expand along the row or column with the most zeros

blocks.prompt: 43 Expanding along the first row, \(|A|\) equals:
blocks.explanation: With minors the signs of row 1 are \(+, -, +\) (formula (v)). With cofactors all signs are plus: \(a_{11}A_{11} + a_{12}A_{12} + a_{13}A_{13}\).

book_ref.quote: Similarly (i) can be written as

blocks.prompt: 44 The values of \(x\) for which \(\begin{vmatrix}x & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & x & 3 \\ 1 & 0 & x\end{vmatrix} = 0\) are:
blocks.explanation: Expand along column 2 (two zeros): only \(a_{22} = x\) remains, \(x\begin{vmatrix}x & 1 \\ 1 & x\end{vmatrix} = x(x^{2} - 1) = 0\), so \(x = 0, 1, -1\).

book_ref.quote: a zero element makes its whole term vanish

blocks.prompt: 45 For a square matrix \(A\), \(|A^{t}|\) equals:
blocks.explanation: Property i: \(|A| = |A^{t}|\); transposing does not change the determinant.

book_ref.quote: Transposing: value unchanged

blocks.prompt: 46 If two rows of a square matrix \(A\) are interchanged, the new determinant is:
blocks.explanation: Property ii: interchanging two rows (or two columns) changes the sign: \(-|A|\).

book_ref.quote: two rows or two columns are interchanged, the determinant of the resulting matrix is

blocks.prompt: 47 The value of \(\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 6 \\ 5 & 7 & 9\end{vmatrix}\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(R_{2} = 2R_{1}\). Taking the factor 2 out of \(R_{2}\) (property v) leaves two identical rows, so the value is 0 (property iii).

book_ref.quote: has two identical rows or two identical columns, then

blocks.prompt: 48 If \(|A| = 5\) and every entry of one row of \(A\) is multiplied by 3, the new determinant is:
blocks.explanation: Property v: multiplying one row by \(k\) gives \(k|A| = 3(5) = 15\). (\(135\) would be \(|3A| = 27|A|\).)

book_ref.quote: are multiplied by a number

blocks.prompt: 49 If \(A\) is a square matrix of order 3 with \(|A| = 4\), then \(|2A|\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(2A\) multiplies all three rows by 2, so \(|2A| = 2^{3}|A| = 8 \times 4 = 32\). Taking 2 out only once gives the wrong value 8.

book_ref.quote: Taking \(k\) out of the whole matrix

blocks.prompt: 50 The value of \(\begin{vmatrix}2 & 7 & -1 \\ 0 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\) is:
blocks.explanation: The matrix is upper triangular, so the determinant is the product of the main-diagonal entries: \(2 \times (-3) \times 4 = -24\).

book_ref.quote: If a matrix is in triangular form, then the value of its determinant is the product of the entries on its main diagonal.

blocks.prompt: 51 The operation \(R_{2} + 3R_{1} \to R_{2}\) changes the value of a determinant \(|A|\) to:
blocks.explanation: Property vii: adding \(k\) times one row to another row leaves the determinant unchanged.

book_ref.quote: the value of the determinant does not change

blocks.prompt: 52 If every entry of the third column of a square matrix \(A\) of order 3 is zero, then \(|A|\) is:

options.text: the product of the diagonal entries

blocks.explanation: Property iv: expand along the zero column; every term has a factor 0, so \(|A| = 0\).

book_ref.quote: If all the entries of a row (or a column) of a square matrix

blocks.prompt: 53 The adjoint \(\operatorname{adj} A\) of a square matrix \(A\) is:

options.text: the transpose of the matrix of cofactors

blocks.explanation: \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors: the cofactors of row 1 of \(A\) stand in column 1 of \(\operatorname{adj} A\).

book_ref.quote: is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. The cofactors of row 1

blocks.prompt: 54 A square matrix \(A\) has a multiplicative inverse if and only if:
blocks.explanation: \(A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{|A|}\operatorname{adj} A\) needs division by \(|A|\), so \(A\) must be non-singular: \(|A| \ne 0\).

book_ref.quote: is called the multiplicative inverse of

book_ref.quote: is called singular and has no inverse

blocks.prompt: 56 For a square matrix \(A\) of order 3, \(A(\operatorname{adj} A)\) equals:
blocks.explanation: Each diagonal entry is a row times its own cofactors \(= |A|\); off-diagonal entries are 0. So \(A(\operatorname{adj} A) = |A|\,I\).

book_ref.quote: Multiply \(A\) by \(\operatorname{adj} A\).

blocks.prompt: 58 For \(A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\), \(|A| = 1\). The entry in row 1, column 2 of \(A^{-1}\) is:
blocks.explanation: Row 1, column 2 of \(\operatorname{adj} A\) is the cofactor \(A_{21} = -\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} = -(8 - 3) = -5\); divide by \(|A| = 1\). (\(A_{12} = 2\) would be the slip of not transposing.)

book_ref.quote: Write the matrix of cofactors and take its transpose

blocks.text: 4.6 Elementary Row Operations on a Matrix

blocks.prompt: 59 Which of the following is NOT an elementary row operation?

options.text: adding 2 times one row to another row

blocks.explanation: The three elementary row operations are: interchange two rows, multiply a row by a non-zero number, add a multiple of one row to another. Multiplying by 0 would wipe out an equation.

book_ref.quote: Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

blocks.prompt: 60 A square matrix \(A = [a_{ij}]\) is upper triangular if:
blocks.explanation: Upper triangular: all elements below the principal diagonal are zero, i.e. \(a_{ij} = 0\) for \(i > j\) (row number bigger than column number).

book_ref.quote: is called an upper triangular matrix if all elements below the principal diagonal are zero

blocks.prompt: 61 Which of the following is a lower triangular matrix?
blocks.explanation: Lower triangular: all elements above the principal diagonal are zero (\(a_{12} = a_{13} = a_{23} = 0\)). The first distractor is upper triangular.

book_ref.quote: is said to be lower triangular matrix if all elements above the principal diagonal are zero

blocks.prompt: 62 A diagonal matrix is:
blocks.explanation: In a diagonal matrix every entry off the diagonal is zero, so the entries both below and above the diagonal are zero.

book_ref.quote: Diagonal matrices are both upper triangular and lower triangular.

blocks.prompt: 63 Adding \(k\) times \(R_{j}\) to \(R_{i}\) is written as:
blocks.explanation: The changed row is written first and on the right of the arrow: \(R_{i} + kR_{j} \to R_{i}'\); \(R_{j}\) itself stays the same.

book_ref.quote: can be obtained by applying in turn a finite number of row operations on

blocks.text: 4.7 Echelon and Reduced Echelon Forms of Matrices

blocks.prompt: 64 The leading entry of the row \(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & -3 & 5\end{bmatrix}\) is:
blocks.explanation: The leading entry is the first non-zero entry of a non-zero row, read from the left: \(-3\).

book_ref.quote: the first non-zero entry is called the leading entry of that row

blocks.prompt: 65 Which of the following matrices is in echelon form?
blocks.explanation: It has leading entries 1, more zeros before each leading entry than in the row above, and the zero row last. The others fail: a leading 3, a zero row on top, two rows starting with no zeros.

book_ref.quote: (or leading entry) in each row is 1

blocks.prompt: 66 In the reduced (row) echelon form, the column containing a leading 1 has:
blocks.explanation: Reduced echelon form: if the leading entry of \(R_{i}\) lies in \(C_{j}\), all other entries of \(C_{j}\) are zero (above and below).

book_ref.quote: then all other entries of

blocks.prompt: 67 The rank of \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 6\end{bmatrix}\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(R_{2} + (-3)R_{1}\) gives the zero row \((0, 0)\), so the echelon form has one non-zero row: rank 1.

book_ref.quote: is the number of non-zero rows when it is reduced to the echelon form

blocks.prompt: 68 The rank of \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}\) is:

book_ref.quote: If \(r\) is the number of non-zero rows

blocks.prompt: 69 To find \(A^{-1}\) by row operations, \(A \vdots I\) is reduced to:
blocks.explanation: Row operations that turn \(A\) into \(I\) turn \(I\) into \(A^{-1}\): \(A \vdots I \to I \vdots A^{-1}\).

book_ref.quote: If the application of elementary row operations on

blocks.prompt: 70 The rank of a \(3 \times 5\) matrix can be at most:
blocks.explanation: The rank of an \(m \times n\) matrix is never more than the smaller of \(m\) and \(n\): here \(3\).

book_ref.quote: The rank of an \(m \times n\) matrix is never more than the smaller of

blocks.prompt: 71 A system of linear equations is non-homogeneous if its constant terms are:
blocks.explanation: System (i) is non-homogeneous if the constant terms \(d_{1}, d_{2}, d_{3}\) are not all zero; if all are zero it is homogeneous.

book_ref.quote: is called a system of non-homogeneous linear equations in the three variables

blocks.prompt: 72 A system of linear equations is called consistent if it has:

options.text: a unique solution or infinitely many solutions

blocks.explanation: Consistent: a unique solution or infinitely many solutions. Inconsistent: no solution.

book_ref.quote: is said to be consistent if the system has a unique solution or it has infinitely many solutions

blocks.prompt: 73 The system \(x + y = 2,\ x + y = 3\) is:
blocks.explanation: No pair can make \(x + y\) equal both 2 and 3 (parallel lines), so there is no solution: inconsistent.

book_ref.quote: is said to be inconsistent if the system has no solution

blocks.prompt: 74 While solving a system, the reduced augmented matrix has the row \(\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{array}\right]\). The system:
blocks.explanation: The row means \(0x + 0y + 0z = 5\), i.e. \(0 = 5\), which is impossible: the system is inconsistent.

book_ref.quote: Solve by back substitution

blocks.prompt: 75 For a system in 3 variables, rank of the coefficient matrix = rank of the augmented matrix = 2. The system has:
blocks.explanation: Equal ranks less than the number of variables (\(2 < 3\)): consistent with infinitely many solutions.

book_ref.quote: Thus a system is consistent and has infinitely many solutions if the two ranks are equal but less than the number of variables.

blocks.prompt: 76 The system \(x + y - z = 2,\ 2x + 3y + z = 7,\ 3x + 4y = 10\) is:
blocks.explanation: Adding the first two equations gives \(3x + 4y = 9\), which contradicts \(3x + 4y = 10\). In echelon form a row \((0, 0, 0 \mid 1)\) appears: rank of \(A\) is 2, rank of the augmented matrix is 3.

book_ref.quote: Thus a system is inconsistent if the ranks of the coefficient matrix and the augmented matrix are different.

blocks.prompt: 77 The augmented matrix of \(x + 2y = 5,\ 3x - y = 1\) (two equations) is:
blocks.explanation: Each row is one equation: the coefficients of x and y, then the constant after the bar. The last distractor is only the coefficient matrix.

book_ref.quote: Convert to augmented matrix

blocks.prompt: 78 If a system is written as \(AX = B\) with \(|A| \ne 0\), then \(X\) equals:
blocks.explanation: Multiply \(AX = B\) on the left by \(A^{-1}\): \(A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B\), so \(X = A^{-1}B\). \(BA^{-1}\) is not even defined for a column \(B\).

book_ref.quote: The matrix inversion method is a way to solve a system of linear equations using the inverse of a matrix.

blocks.prompt: 79 The matrix inversion method cannot be used when:
blocks.explanation: \(A^{-1}\) exists only when \(|A| \ne 0\). For \(|A| = 0\) the echelon method is used instead.

book_ref.quote: Check \(|A| \ne 0\); otherwise the method cannot be used.

blocks.prompt: 80 By Cramer's rule, \(x_{2} = \dfrac{D_{2}}{|A|}\), where \(D_{2}\) is \(|A|\) with:
blocks.explanation: From (iv): \(x_{2}\) has numerator \(\begin{vmatrix}a_{11} & b_{1} & a_{13} \\ a_{21} & b_{2} & a_{23} \\ a_{31} & b_{3} & a_{33}\end{vmatrix}\): the second column replaced by \(b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}\).

book_ref.quote: is often referred to as Cramer's Rule

blocks.prompt: 81 For \(x - y + z = 2,\ 2x + y - z = 1,\ x + 2y + 2z = 11\), \(|A| = 12\). By Cramer's rule \(x\) is:

book_ref.quote: with coefficients and constant terms in the real field

blocks.prompt: 82 Cramer's rule gives a unique solution of a system of three equations only when:
blocks.explanation: \(x_{k} = \dfrac{D_{k}}{|A|}\) needs division by \(|A|\), so \(|A| \ne 0\) is required; then the solution is unique.

book_ref.quote: These are three linear equations in three variables

blocks.prompt: 83 A homogeneous system of linear equations is always:
blocks.explanation: \(x_{1} = x_{2} = x_{3} = 0\) always satisfies it, so a homogeneous system is always consistent.

book_ref.quote: so such a system is always consistent

blocks.prompt: 84 The trivial solution of a homogeneous system in three variables is:
blocks.explanation: The solution \((0, 0, 0)\) is the trivial solution; any other solution is non-trivial.

book_ref.quote: of the above homogeneous system is called the trivial solution

blocks.prompt: 85 If the coefficient matrix \(A\) of a homogeneous system \(AX = O\) has \(|A| \ne 0\), the system has:
blocks.explanation: If \(|A| \ne 0\), \(A^{-1}\) exists and \(X = A^{-1}O = O\): only the trivial solution.

book_ref.quote: Any other solution of system (i) other than the trivial solution is called a non-trivial solution.

blocks.text: 4.9.1 Solution of System of Homogeneous Linear Equations by Gaussian Elimination Method

blocks.prompt: 86 Gaussian elimination is named after:
blocks.explanation: Gaussian Elimination is named after the German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss.

blocks.prompt: 87 A homogeneous system in 3 variables whose coefficient matrix has rank 2 has:
blocks.explanation: Rule II: rank \(<\) number of variables (\(2 < 3\)) gives non-trivial solutions; one variable is free.

blocks.prompt: 88 The value of \(\lambda\) for which \(x + 2y + z = 0,\ 2x - y + 3z = 0,\ 3x + y + \lambda z = 0\) has a non-trivial solution is:
blocks.explanation: Non-trivial solutions need rank \(< 3\), i.e. \(|A| = 0\): \(1(-\lambda - 3) - 2(2\lambda - 9) + 1(2 + 3) = -5\lambda + 20 = 0\), so \(\lambda = 4\).

blocks.prompt: 89 After Gaussian elimination a homogeneous system becomes \(x + y - z = 0,\ y + 2z = 0,\ z = 0\). Its solution is:
blocks.explanation: Back substitution: \(z = 0\), then \(y = -2z = 0\), then \(x = -y + z = 0\). Only the trivial solution.

blocks.explanation: \(\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\): \(x\) stays, the sign of \(y\) changes.

blocks.prompt: 91 The matrix that reflects a point in the line \(y = x\) is:
blocks.explanation: \(\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}y \\ x\end{bmatrix}\): it swaps the coordinates. The next two reflect in the \(x\)-axis and the \(y\)-axis.

blocks.prompt: 93 Using \(A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(A = 1, \ldots, Z = 26\), the letters HE are coded as:
blocks.explanation: H = 8, E = 5: \(\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}16 + 5 \\ 8 + 5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}21 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}\).

book_ref.quote: Coding is the process of converting a message into a specific format using a code.

blocks.prompt: 94 To decode a message coded with matrix A, the coded matrix is multiplied by:
blocks.explanation: If \(Y = AX\), then \(A^{-1}Y = A^{-1}AX = X\): decoding uses the inverse of the coding matrix.

book_ref.quote: To decode a message, we multiply coded matrix by the inverse of the given matrix.

blocks.prompt: 95 Which matrix cannot be used as a code matrix?
blocks.explanation: \(\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} = 4 - 4 = 0\), so it has no inverse and the message could not be decoded. The other determinants are \(1\), \(-5\), \(1\).
